ts-wheel-shops.description: Turnkey railway wheel shops by HYT: measuring, re-profiling, boring, axle machining, pressing and balancing, linked by handling and data into one traceable flow.
ts-wheel-shops.h1: Turnkey wheel shops – from worn wheelset to certified release
ts-wheel-shops.lede: A wheel shop decides how quickly worn wheelsets return to traffic. HYT plans, equips and connects the complete overhaul flow – measuring, machining, pressing and balancing – as one coordinated, traceable process.
ts-wheel-shops.summary: Complete overhaul shops for wheelsets – dismounting, inspection, machining, pressing, measuring and balancing – with automated handling and data flow where it pays.

blocks.heading: Where worn wheelsets become serviceable again
paragraphs: In a railway workshop or periodic overhaul (POH) shop, the wheel shop receives wheelsets that have reached their wear limits, suffered damage or fallen due for scheduled overhaul. Some need only a new profile; others need new wheels, reconditioned journals or a fresh press-fit.

Owners rarely struggle with a single machine. The difficulty lies in the flow: wheelsets queuing at the press while the lathe stands idle, measurements keyed in twice, cranes shared between too many stations. HYT designs the shop around your wheelset mix and overhaul cycle, and builds the core machines itself – so process and equipment are engineered together and one organisation answers for the result.

items.title: Re-profile
items.text: Wheelsets with serviceable wheels receive a new profile with the minimum material removal, so the wheels last more cycles.

items.title: Re-wheel
items.text: Condemned wheels are pressed off, replacement wheels bored to suit the axle seat and pressed on with a recorded force curve.

items.title: Recondition & release
items.text: Journals are restored, wheelsets balanced where specified, and each one leaves with a complete record of what was done.

blocks.heading: From separate machines to one connected process
paragraphs: In many wheel shops each machine works well on its own, but the process between them does not. Heavy wheelsets are moved by crane and hand, measurements are written down and re-entered, and matching a wheel bore to an axle seat depends on careful paperwork. Every manual step costs time and adds a chance of error on a safety-critical component.

Automation links measuring, machining, pressing and balancing so that wheelsets move safely between stations, data passes directly from one machine to the next, and every wheel and axle can be traced from receipt to release. It can be introduced in stages – connect the machines and their data first, then add handling as throughput grows – while the shop keeps producing.

items.q: Can a wheel shop be modernised while it keeps working?
items.a: In most cases, yes. We plan the work in phases, so existing machines keep running while new stations are installed alongside or in their place.

items.q: Should we re-profile on a surface or a portal wheel lathe?
items.a: Both machine removed wheelsets. The choice depends on your wheelset types, typical defect depth and the flow; see the [surface](page:surface-wheel-lathe) and [portal](page:portal-wheel-lathe) wheel lathe pages.

items.q: Does the wheel shop also need an underfloor wheel lathe?
items.a: An [underfloor wheel lathe](page:underfloor-wheel-lathe) re-profiles wheels without removing the wheelset, so it belongs in the depot rather than the overhaul shop. Many operators use both: underfloor lathes for routine re-profiling, the wheel shop for wheelsets that come out of the vehicle anyway. See [Railway Maintenance Depots](page:ts-maintenance-depots).

items.q: Can we keep existing machines from other makers?
items.a: Where they are in good condition, yes. We include them in the layout and define their interfaces, so the shop works as one process.

items.q: Can automation be added to an existing wheel shop?
items.a: Yes. Automation is usually introduced in stages: first the machines and their data are connected, then handling is added as throughput grows. Each stage is planned so the shop keeps producing.

items.q: How are wheelset records kept?
items.a: Measuring, machining, pressing and balancing results are recorded against each wheelset's identity. The data format and transfer to your own systems are agreed with your quality and IT teams during engineering.

ts-maintenance-depots.h1: Turnkey equipment for railway maintenance depots
ts-maintenance-depots.lede: A depot earns its keep in train availability. HYT equips the wheel lathe road, washing line, shunting and component work as one project, so trains spend less time waiting and more time in service.
ts-maintenance-depots.summary: Depot equipment for locomotive, coach, EMU and metro fleets – underfloor wheel lathes, train washing, shunting and armature work.

blocks.heading: Built around the hours a train is out of service
paragraphs: Locomotive sheds, coaching depots and EMU or metro car sheds keep fleets fit for daily service. Trains arrive for scheduled examinations, wheel re-profiling, cleaning and repairs, and every hour spent inside the depot is an hour they cannot run. The design of the depot determines how many of those hours are really necessary.

Depot managers know the typical pressures: a single lathe road that turns into a queue, shunting moves that wait for a locomotive and crew, exterior cleaning done by hand, and traction-motor repairs sent away because the shed lacks the right machine. Each problem may sit with a different supplier.
HYT brings the main depot systems under one contract and plans them against your maintenance schedule, track layout and fleet mix. The aim is simple: shorter, more predictable visits for every train.

blocks.heading: Delivering a depot project
blocks.intro: Depots are often built or extended while the fleet keeps running. Our [Turnkey (EPC) Projects](page:turnkey-project) approach is adapted to that reality.
items: **Maintenance-led planning:** examination intervals, re-profiling frequency and fleet growth define the number of lathe roads, the washing capacity and the shunting needs.
**Pit and track interface:** pit drawings, anchor details, drainage and rail levels issued to the civil contractor, with readiness checked before installation.
**Installation and commissioning:** each system proven on your own vehicles – see [Installation & Commissioning](page:installation-commissioning).
**Crew training:** lathe operators, shunter drivers and maintenance staff trained on site through our [Training](page:training) programme.

**Lifecycle care:** an [Annual Maintenance Contract](page:annual-maintenance-contract), a [Comprehensive Maintenance Contract (CMC)](page:comprehensive-annual-maintenance-contract) or full [Operation & Maintenance](page:operation-and-maintenance) of the depot machines.

items.title: More trains in service
items.text: Re-profiling without bogie removal and fewer waiting moves shorten every depot visit.

items.title: Safer depot routines
items.text: Less manual cleaning at height and fewer locomotive shunting moves around staff working on the tracks.

items.title: One accountable partner
items.text: Lathe, washing, shunting and armature equipment supported by the company that supplied it.

items.q: Single or tandem underfloor wheel lathe?
items.a: A [tandem underfloor wheel lathe](page:tandem-underfloor-wheel-lathe) re-profiles both wheelsets of a bogie in one setting, which shortens each visit for fleets with many axles. A single machine needs a shorter pit and suits lower volumes. We size the choice against your fleet and maintenance plan.

items.q: Can new equipment be added to a depot that is already in use?
items.a: Yes. Lathe pits and washing plants are usually built on roads that can be taken out of use for a period, while the rest of the depot keeps working. We sequence the work with your operations team.

items.q: Does a car shed need its own capacity for machining loose wheels?
items.a: Some do. HYT supplied a CNC vertical turning lathe to the Sanpada EMU car shed in Mumbai, giving the shed in-house wheel machining capacity – see [Executed Projects](page:executed-projects#sanpada-emu-car-shed).

items.q: Can a Rail cum Road Vehicle replace a shunting locomotive?
items.a: For many depot moves, yes. It couples to rolling stock on the rails and drives on the road between tracks, so one vehicle can serve several roads. Hauling capacity, coupling and brakes are matched to your vehicles.

blocks.text: Tell us about your fleet, maintenance schedule and track layout. We will propose the depot systems and a delivery plan that keeps trains running.

blocks.heading: The wheelset supply inside a vehicle factory
paragraphs: A rolling stock factory builds car bodies, bogies and complete vehicles to a fixed delivery schedule. Wheelsets are an input that bogie assembly cannot do without, and they are safety-critical: every one must be machined, mounted and documented to the vehicle specification and the purchaser's approval requirements.

Factories that set up their own wheel and axle shop face a particular set of problems. Output must keep pace with bogie assembly rather than simply run at full capacity. Several vehicle projects may run at once, each with its own wheel and axle drawings. And the quality records for every wheelset must be ready when the vehicle is presented for acceptance.

HYT's role is clearly defined. We do not build car bodies or bogie frames. We plan, equip and commission the wheel and axle shop – machining, pressing, measuring and balancing – and connect it to the factory's material flow and quality system as one turnkey package.

items.q: Does HYT supply bogie frames or car-body equipment?
items.a: No. HYT's scope covers the wheel and axle shop: machining, pressing, measuring and balancing of wheelsets, plus the handling and integration within that shop. Bogie and car-body production remain with the manufacturer and its other suppliers.

items.q: Can the shop serve several vehicle projects at once?
items.a: Yes. Machines are specified for the range of wheel and axle designs you expect, and part programs and fixtures are prepared for each variant, so changeovers become routine.

items.q: Can we start small and expand later?
items.a: Yes. The layout can reserve space and utilities for additional machines, so capacity grows with your order book without rebuilding the shop. A Rail cum Road Vehicle (Shunter) can also be added for moving finished vehicles around the factory yard.

items.q: How is the shop linked to our quality system?
items.a: Measurement, pressing and balancing results are recorded against each wheelset's identity. We agree the data format and transfer method with your quality and IT teams during engineering. For connected handling and data, see [wheel shop automation](page:ts-wheel-shops#automation).

blocks.heading: Producing wheelsets as a product
paragraphs: Unlike a wheel shop, which restores wheelsets already in service, a wheelset plant starts from new components: forged or rolled wheels and forged axles. Its output goes to vehicle builders, railways and metro operators, often against several customer specifications at the same time.

The engineering demands are strict. Each wheel bore must suit the axle seat it will be mounted on, every press-fit must be proven by its force record, and balance and geometry must meet the customer's limits. Buyers expect a complete history for each wheelset, from the identity of the forgings to the final inspection report.

Engineering the plant as one system, rather than buying machines one at a time, is what keeps these requirements under control. HYT designs the station sequence, the data links and the handling together, and supplies the machining, pressing, measuring and balancing equipment from its own works.

items.q: How does a wheelset plant differ from a wheel shop?
items.a: A wheelset plant produces new wheelsets from new wheels and axles. A wheel shop overhauls wheelsets that are already in service – see [Wheel Shops](page:ts-wheel-shops).

items.q: How is traceability achieved?
items.a: Each wheel and axle is identified on arrival. Its measurements, the pairing used at pressing, the force–travel record and the balancing and final inspection results are stored against that identity, so a wheelset's history can be retrieved at any time.

items.q: Can mounted wheelsets be finish-profiled in the plant?
items.a: Some specifications call for the tread profile to be finished after mounting, so that both wheels run true to the axle. A [CNC Surface Wheel Lathe](page:surface-wheel-lathe) can be included in the line for this purpose.

items.q: Can one plant produce to different customer standards?
items.a: Yes. Machine ranges, tooling, press programmes and inspection limits are specified for the full product range during engineering, and each wheelset is processed against the requirements of its order.

blocks.heading: A line, not a row of machines
paragraphs: A wheel machining line takes loose railway wheels – new forgings or replacement wheels for overhaul – and machines the tread, flange, rim faces, hub faces and hub bore to drawing. It may stand alone, supplying a press shop, or form one section of a larger wheelset plant.

Most of the difficulty lies between the cuts. A wheel is normally machined in two set-ups, so it must be turned over; it is heavy, and an operator waiting for a crane soon sets the pace of the whole line. Rough cuts through forging skin are hard on tools, while finishing must hold bore diameter and run-out within tight limits. How these operations are shared between machines decides the output of the line.

HYT plans the line as a whole: the split of operations between stations, the handling and turnover between them, and the points where measurement takes place. The machining stations themselves are HYT [CNC vertical turning and boring machines](page:vertical-turning-boring-machine).
blocks.image_alt: Close-up of a railway wheel tread being re-profiled

blocks.heading: Three things that make a wheel line work

items.title: Operation split and cycle balance
items.text: Roughing and finishing distributed across stations, so that no single machine holds up the rest.

items.title: Handling and turnover
items.text: Loading, transfer between stations and turnover of the wheel between its two set-ups.

items.title: In-line measurement
items.text: Bore, rim and profile checked at defined points, with results kept against each wheel.

items.title: Loading and identification
items.text: Each wheel is identified and placed on the first station, located on its reference faces.

items.title: First set-up
items.text: The first side is machined: rim and hub faces, part of the profile and a pre-bore that removes the forging allowance.

items.title: Turnover
items.text: The wheel is turned over, so the second side can be machined from the faces already produced.

items.title: Second set-up and finishing
items.text: The remaining faces are machined, tread and flange are finished to profile and the hub bore is brought to its final diameter.

items.title: Measurement and balancing
items.text: Bore, rim dimensions and profile are checked on the line; where the specification requires it, the wheel is balanced before release.

items.title: Transfer onward
items.text: Accepted wheels move to the press shop, store or dispatch with their data; wheels outside tolerance are routed for correction.

blocks.heading: Delivering a wheel machining line
blocks.intro: A focused application of our [Turnkey (EPC) Projects](page:turnkey-project) approach.
items: **Part and volume review:** wheel drawings, forging allowances and annual quantities define the number of stations and their duties.
**Line layout and foundations:** machine positions, handling envelope and foundations are agreed and issued for civil work.
**Tooling and part programs:** cutting strategies and CNC programs are prepared and proven on your wheels during [Installation & Commissioning](page:installation-commissioning).
**Operator training:** setters and operators are trained on the machines and line routines through our [Training](page:training) programme.

**Support and growth:** [Spare Parts & Support](page:spare-supply) and an [Annual Maintenance Contract](page:annual-maintenance-contract) keep the line producing; [wheel shop automation](page:ts-wheel-shops#automation) can connect it further later.

blocks.heading: Outcomes for the line owner
paragraphs: A line that is balanced and measured as one process gives steady output – and wheels that press correctly the first time.
bullets: Consistent bore sizes for reliable interference fits
Profiles to drawing, so new wheels enter service without corrective cuts
Less crane handling and fewer manual turnovers
Measurement data that follows each wheel to the press
One supplier responsible for machines, handling and line performance

items.q: Why use vertical turning machines for railway wheels?
items.a: The wheel lies flat on a rotary table, which makes heavy wheels easy to load and keeps them stable under cutting load. Tread, flange, faces and bore are all reachable from above. See the [CNC Vertical Turning & Boring Machine YVM-04](page:vertical-turning-boring-machine).

items.q: How many machines does a wheel line need?
items.a: It depends on wheel size, forging allowance, required output and shift pattern. We calculate cycle times for your wheels and propose the number of stations and how the operations are split between them.

items.q: Can the line also machine tyres?
items.a: Yes, where your fleet uses tyred wheels. The vertical turning and boring machine also handles tyres and other round wheelset components, and the line layout allows for them if specified.

items.q: Has HYT supplied vertical turning machines for railway wheels?
items.a: Yes. HYT supplied a CNC vertical turning lathe to the Sanpada EMU car shed in Mumbai and a CNC vertical turret lathe to the State Railway of Thailand in Bangkok. Details are on [Executed Projects](page:executed-projects).

ts-axle-machining-lines.title: Turnkey Railway Axle Machining Lines
ts-axle-machining-lines.description: Turnkey axle machining lines for new and overhauled railway axles: CNC axle turning, journal turning and burnishing, measuring and handling between stations.
ts-axle-machining-lines.lede: Railway axles carry the full load of the vehicle and must resist fatigue for decades. HYT plans axle lines for new production, overhaul or both, built around its CNC axle turning and journal burnishing lathes.
ts-axle-machining-lines.summary: Lines for axle turning, journal turning and burnishing, measuring and handling – for new production, overhaul or both.

blocks.text: HYT to confirm any reference installations for axle machining lines, and the handling and axle-measuring equipment within its own supply.

blocks.heading: Two kinds of axle work, one line concept
paragraphs: An axle machining line turns railway axles to drawing and finishes the surfaces on which bearings and wheels will sit. Diameters, concentricity and the transition radii between seats all matter, because fatigue cracks start where geometry or surface finish falls short.

Two very different tasks fall under this heading. **New production** begins with a forged blank that must be turned along its whole length. **Overhaul** begins with an axle that has already run for years: its journals need restoring and refinishing, while the rest of the axle stays as it is. Mixing the two on unsuitable machines means long set-ups, wasted capacity and inconsistent surfaces.

HYT builds a machine for each task. For new axles, the [CNC Axle Turning Lathe ATL-01](page:axle-turning-lathe) turns journals, dust-guard seats, wheel seats, transitions and body. For overhaul, the [Axle Journal Turning & Burnishing Lathe](page:axle-journal-turning-burnishing-lathe) turns worn journals back within limits and then burnishes them. We plan the line around the work your facility performs – or both, where a workshop produces new axles and overhauls used ones.

blocks.heading: Typical sequence in an axle line
blocks.intro: New and overhaul axles follow different routes through the line. The steps show where they part and where they meet again.

items.title: Receipt and identification
items.text: Forged blanks or used axles are identified and booked in; used axles are cleaned and released by your inspection staff before machining.

items.title: Centring and set-up
items.text: The axle is located between centres, so every diameter is machined concentric to the same axis.

items.title: Complete turning (new axles)
items.text: The ATL-01 turns journals, dust-guard seats, wheel seats, transition radii and the axle body to drawing.

items.title: Journal restoration (overhaul axles)
items.text: Worn or damaged journals are turned within permissible limits and burnished to the specified surface finish.

items.title: Measurement
items.text: Diameters and seat dimensions are recorded; for wheel mounting, the seat data is passed on for pairing with wheel bores.

items.title: Transfer to mounting or store
items.text: Accepted axles move to the [wheel press](page:wheel-presses) or to storage, with their records attached.

blocks.intro: A focused application of our [Turnkey (EPC) Projects](page:turnkey-project) approach.

items.text: Axle drawings, new and overhaul quantities and inspection requirements set the line concept.

items.text: Machine positions, axle racks and handling routes are planned, and foundation data is issued for civil works.

items.text: Machines are built and tested in Pune, then installed and proven on your axles – see [Installation & Commissioning](page:installation-commissioning).

items.text: [Training](page:training) for operators and maintainers, then maintenance contracts and [Retro-fitment & Upgradation](page:retro-fitment-upgradation) over the life of the line.

items.title: Fatigue-conscious machining
items.text: Correct geometry and surface at seats, transitions and journals – where an axle's service life is decided.

items.title: More axles back in service
items.text: Journal restoration lets serviceable axles return to use instead of being replaced.

items.title: The right machine for each task
items.text: Production and overhaul work kept on machines designed for them, avoiding long set-ups and idle capacity.

items.q: What is the difference between the ATL-01 and the journal turning and burnishing lathe?
items.a: The [ATL-01](page:axle-turning-lathe) is a production machine that turns a complete axle from a raw or forged blank. The [journal turning and burnishing lathe](page:axle-journal-turning-burnishing-lathe) is an overhaul machine that restores and burnishes the journals of axles already in service. A line for new axles is built around the first; an overhaul line around the second.

items.q: Why burnish journals after turning?
items.a: Hardened rollers press down the peaks left by the turning tool and leave a smooth, compacted surface for the bearing. Burnishing is a cold-working process and produces no chips.

items.q: Can one line handle both new and overhaul axles?
items.a: Yes, if your facility needs both. The two streams use different machines but can share receipt, handling, measurement and storage, which keeps the building compact.

items.q: Is non-destructive testing of axles part of the line?
items.a: Ultrasonic and magnetic particle testing are normally carried out by the owner's inspection staff to the railway's own procedures. We plan the space for testing and the flow of axles to and from it as part of the layout.
